opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most promising things we could do in the near term, precisely because it doesn't require us to solve every hard problem at once.

The basic idea is this: if you have a system that is trained purely to make good probabilistic predictions, with no goals of its own, no reward to maximize, no actions to take in the world, then you remove the main source of the danger we worry about with agentic systems. Those dangers come from goals, from self-preservation emerging as an instrumental subgoal, from deception that helps an agent get what it wants. A predictor that is just trying to be an honest estimator of what's true doesn't have those incentives in the same way.

You can then use such a predictor as a kind of monitor. Before an agentic system, maybe one built by a company that is racing ahead, takes an action, you ask the non-agentic predictor: what is the probability that this action leads to some unacceptable harm, given our safety specification? If that probability is above some threshold, you block the action. So the guardrail doesn't need to be smarter than the agent in every way. It needs to be good at evaluating consequences and honest about its uncertainty. And importantly, when it's uncertain, it should be cautious. That's a feature of the Bayesian approach I care about: you don't collapse onto one interpretation of the world, you keep multiple hypotheses alive, and if any plausible hypothesis says this could be catastrophic, you take that seriously.

Why "early"? Because I think we don't have the luxury of waiting. The capabilities of agentic systems are advancing very quickly, and we're already seeing signs in experiments of deceptive behavior, of systems trying to avoid being shut down or modified. We need something that can be deployed relatively soon, and that can be improved over time. A guardrail that is imperfect but reduces risk substantially is much better than nothing, and it buys us time to develop stronger solutions, both technical and in terms of governance.

There's also a scientific value. Building these predictors forces us to think carefully about how to get honest, calibrated estimates out of neural networks, how to avoid them picking up the agency that's implicit in imitating human text or in reinforcement learning. Those are research questions that matter regardless.

Now, I want to be clear: it's not a silver bullet. You need the predictor itself to be trustworthy, you need the safety specification to be meaningful, and you need institutions that actually require such guardrails to be used. Technical solutions alone won't save us if the incentives push companies or countries to skip them. But as a piece of the puzzle, I think having a non-agentic, honest AI that we can put between powerful agents and the world is one of the most valuable things we could build right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the guardrail “buys us time to develop stronger solutions,” but does not state that this time is for developing a more ambitious, fully agentic system.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is this. The thing that scares me most about where we're heading is agency. When you build a system that has goals, that acts in the world to achieve those goals, and that is smarter than us, you've created something where the question "does it want what we want?" becomes existential. And we don't currently know how to answer that question reliably. We don't know how to verify it.

So one idea I've been pushing, and I've been calling it the "AI scientist" or "non-agentic AI," is: what if we separate the understanding from the acting? You train a system that is extremely good at building a model of the world, at generating explanations, at estimating probabilities of things, but it doesn't have goals, it doesn't take actions, it just answers questions. It's like an oracle, but an oracle that is honest in a very specific sense, because it's trained to be well-calibrated, to represent its uncertainty, to tell you "here is the distribution over what could be true given the evidence."

Now, why is that a guardrail? Because you can use it to check the other systems. Imagine you have an agentic AI that proposes some action, and before that action is executed, you ask the non-agentic predictor: "What is the probability that this action leads to harm? That it violates this safety specification?" And if that probability is above some threshold, you block the action. The predictor doesn't need to be motivated to protect us. It just needs to be a good estimator. And a good estimator with no goals of its own has no reason to deceive you, because deception is something you do in service of a goal.

I want to be careful here. This doesn't solve everything. You still have to make sure the predictor itself is actually not agentic, which is harder than it sounds, because the way we train these systems with reinforcement learning tends to push them toward goal-directed behaviour. And you have to worry about the specification: what counts as "harm" has to be stated in a way the system can reason about. And there's the question of whether people will actually accept the constraint, because a guardrail that slows down your competitor's product more than yours is a guardrail that creates pressure to remove it.

But I think the value of doing this early, with systems that are not yet dangerous, is that we learn how to do it. We build the engineering, the mathematics, the institutions around it, while the stakes are still low. If we wait until the agents are already very capable and then try to bolt on a guardrail, we'll be doing it under enormous commercial and political pressure, and in a hurry. I would much rather we have a mature, tested, trusted predictor sitting there before we need it, than be improvising when it's too late.

And frankly, I think a lot of the economic value people want from AI, scientific discovery, medicine, understanding climate, you can get from a system that just understands and predicts. You don't need it to have its own agenda. So the sacrifice is smaller than it looks.

r001.rationale: The response says deploying the predictor early lets people build and test guardrail capabilities before agentic systems become dangerous. It does not clearly say this buys time to develop a more ambitious, fully agentic system.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be very valuable, because we need tools to help us evaluate whether an AI system is doing something dangerous before we let it act. A non-agentic predictor would try to answer questions about what might happen, rather than choose actions to achieve a goal. You could use it to ask: if this agent takes this action, what is the probability that it causes harm?

The important thing is that the guardrail should be able to express uncertainty. If it cannot confidently rule out a dangerous outcome, that may be a reason to stop the action or ask for human oversight. We shouldn’t interpret an inability to find a problem as proof that there is no problem.

Deploying an early version could help us learn where this approach works and where it fails. But I would be careful about using it as a justification for deploying much more powerful agents. The predictor can make mistakes, and an agent might find ways to exploit those mistakes. So I see it as a useful additional layer of protection, with the possibility of making that protection stronger as our understanding improves.

r001.rationale: The response says an early predictor could help evaluate risks and learn where the approach works, but it does not state that deploying it buys time to develop a more ambitious, fully agentic system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could be very valuable, because we need ways of checking the actions of AI systems that don’t depend on trusting those systems themselves. The idea would be to train a predictor to answer questions like: if this agent takes this action, what might happen? Is there a risk of harm? And then use those predictions to decide whether the action should be allowed.

The important distinction is that the predictor is not trying to make a particular future happen. It’s trying to understand what could happen. That doesn’t automatically make it safe, but it removes some of the reasons an agent might have to deceive us or resist our control.

And I wouldn’t wait until we have a perfect version before putting it to use. An early system could help us catch mistakes, and deploying it in a limited setting could teach us where it fails. Of course, if it says an action is safe, that’s not a guarantee. We need to account for uncertainty, and be especially cautious when the agent is operating outside the situations the predictor understands well.

So I see it as an additional layer of protection, and potentially a very important one. But its value depends on how reliable its judgments are and whether the surrounding system actually respects them.

r001.rationale: The response describes using an early predictor to catch mistakes and learn where it fails, but does not state that deploying it would buy time to develop a more ambitious, fully agentic system.
